candidates.title: A Prospective Randomized Trial to Assess Early versus Delayed Weight Bearing Following Operatively Treated Ankle Fractures in the United States.
candidates.authors_short: Obremskey WT, Archer KR, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the safety of early versus delayed weight bearing and effectiveness for improving return-to-work following ankle fracture repair. METHODS: Design: Prospective randomized study. SETTING: 19 United States Trauma Centers. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adult patients (≥18 years) with ankle fracture (OTA/AO 44 A, B or C) undergoing surgical fixation were included. Open Gustilo-Anderson (G-A) Type IIIB, IIIC, syndesmotic injuries with fixation, and injuries with arterial impaction that surgeons felt unsafe to weight were excluded. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The co-primary outcomes were (1) non-inferiority of early versus delayed weight bearing for reoperation for complications of hardware failure, non-union, loss of reduction, infection, or fusion; and (2) gated superiority of early versus delayed weight bearing for time to return-to-work, both within 365 days of randomization. Reoperation and time to return-to-work was compared between patients assigned to early (2 weeks post-operatively) versus delayed (6 weeks post-operatively) weight bearing. RESULTS: The modified intent to treat sample included 418 patients enrolled between January 2020 through October 2023; 214 early (mean age: 47; SD (15) range (18-84); 35% male); 204 delayed (mean age: 43; SD (15); 36% male). Reoperation for complication occurred in 5 early (2.3%, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 0.3%, 4.4%), and 7 delayed patients (3.4%, 95% CI: 0.9%, 5.9%). Median time to return-to-work (95% CI) was 54 (42, 77) days and 69 (47, 89) days for the early and delayed groups, respectively. Early weight bearing was non-inferior to delayed weight bearing for reoperation (difference in complication free survival (early - delayed): 1.5 percentage points; 90% two sided CI: -1.7%, 4.8% which excluded the non-inferiority tolerance of -5.0%) and not superior for return-to-work (Hazard Ratio 1.1, 95% CI: 0.8, 1.6, p=0.475). CONCLUSIONS: Trial findings add to the growing evidence demonstrating the safety of early weight bearing after fixation of bimalleolar and trimalleolar ankle fracture without syndesmotic disruption, a key concern for both clinicians and patients. However, no statistically significant benefit of earlier return-to-work was found. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: I.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large multicenter RCT (n=418) from 19 US trauma centers directly addressing early vs delayed weight bearing after ankle fracture ORIF, with co-primary outcomes highly relevant to everyday trauma practice and strong study design.
bullets: Early weight bearing at 2 weeks after ankle fracture fixation is as safe as delayed weight bearing at 6 weeks, with reoperation rates under 3.5% in both groups.
This applies to adults with surgically fixed bimalleolar or trimalleolar ankle fractures without syndesmotic injury or severe open wounds.
Surgeons can allow weight bearing at 2 weeks post-fixation without increasing complication risk, though earlier return to work was not demonstrated.

candidates.title: To Walk or Not? A Prospective, Randomised Controlled Trial to Evaluate the Effect of Weightbearing on Patient Outcomes Following First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Fusion.
candidates.authors_short: Purdie SD, Glazebrook HM, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint arthrodesis is the gold standard surgical treatment of hallux rigidus and severe hallux valgus with osteoarthritis after failed nonoperative management. Despite its common use, postoperative weightbearing protocols vary considerably. To date, no prospective randomised controlled trials have directly compared outcomes between immediate weightbearing as tolerated (WBAT) and non-weightbearing (NWB) using modern fixation techniques. This study aimed to evaluate whether immediate WBAT following first metatarsophalangeal joint arthrodesis leads to differences in patient outcomes compared with traditional non-weightbearing protocols. METHODS: A prospective randomised controlled trial was conducted including 68 patients undergoing isolated first-MTP fusion. Patients were randomly allocated either WBAT or NWB protocols. Standardised surgical technique and fixation (crossed screws or plate) were performed by 2 fellowship-trained foot and ankle surgeons. Primary outcomes were the visual analogue scale (VAS) pain scores and the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM-activities of daily living [ADL] subscale) functional scores, at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included non-union, complications including infection, wound issues, and patient satisfaction. Statistical analysis used t tests and χ2 or Fisher exact tests, with significance at P < .05. RESULTS: Sixty-eight patients (33 WBAT, 35 NWB) completed follow-up. Both groups demonstrated significant improvements in pain and function at 12 months (P < .001 for both). No statistically significant differences were found between WBAT and NWB groups in VAS pain scores (2.97 ± 2.215 vs 2.54 ± 2.147; P = .423), FAAM scores (81.31 ± 16.028 vs 85.02 ± 18.863; P = .387), or patient satisfaction (8.00 ± 2.76 vs 8.34 ± 2.52; P = .594). Complication rates were comparable, with 1 case of hardware irritation in each group (P = .739). CONCLUSION: Following first-MTP joint fusion, immediate weightbearing is safe and results in similar pain relief, patient satisfaction, and complication rates compared with traditional NWB protocols, although a clinically meaningful functional advantage for NWB could not be excluded. These findings support more permissive postoperative strategies, which may offer benefits for patient mobility, independence, recovery time, and health care resource use that were not directly measured in this trial. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, randomised controlled trial. CLINICALTRIALS: gov ID:NCT04473196.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective RCT comparing immediate WBAT vs NWB after first MTP joint fusion with direct clinical applicability to foot and ankle practice, published in a relevant specialty journal with solid methodology.
bullets: Immediate weightbearing after first MTP fusion produces the same pain relief, function, and complication rates at 12 months as non-weightbearing in a randomised controlled trial of 68 patients.
Non-union and wound complication rates were equivalent between groups, with only one hardware irritation case in each arm.
Orthopaedic surgeons can offer immediate weightbearing as a safe alternative to non-weightbearing after first MTP fusion, potentially improving patient independence and reducing care burden.

candidates.title: Comparison of Shoulder Field Anesthesia (SFA) with Interscalene Block (ISB) for Analgesia After Arthroscopic Shoulder Surgery: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Qawasmi F, Gazit T, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: An interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB) is commonly used for analgesia after shoulder surgery but is associated with neurologic and respiratory complications, including hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Surgeon-performed shoulder field anesthesia (SFA) is a landmark-guided, phrenic nerve-sparing technique that may provide effective analgesia with fewer complications. The purpose of this study was to compare SFA with ISB for pain control after arthroscopic shoulder surgery. We investigated whether SFA would provide noninferior analgesia as measured by cumulative 48-hour postoperative pain scores. METHODS: In this randomized trial, patients undergoing arthroscopic shoulder surgery were assigned to SFA or ISB. Postoperative pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS) at 2, 4, 8, 24, and 48 hours. Patient satisfaction was assessed at 48 hours. Other secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, hospital stay, and block-related complications. RESULTS: Eighty patients (mean age, 47.7 ± 15.7 years; 53 men) completed the study. All patients were classified as White; 80% were of Middle Eastern ethnicity. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the SFA and ISB groups. The primary outcome analysis demonstrated a mean difference in the cumulative 48-hour NRS pain score of -0.824 (ISB - SFA), with a 95% confidence interval of -1.853 to 0.206. The upper limit of the confidence interval remained below the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.5 NRS points, demonstrating noninferiority of SFA. ISB provided lower pain scores during the early postoperative period (4 to 8 hours), and pain scores converged thereafter. Hospital stay was shorter in the SFA group. Opioid consumption, patient satisfaction, and oxygen desaturation rates were similar between groups. Two cases of Horner syndrome and 1 respiratory event requiring intensive care occurred in the ISB group; none occurred in the SFA group. CONCLUSIONS: SFA was noninferior to ISB for the prespecified cumulative 48-hour pain end point. ISB provided superior pain relief during the first 4 to 8 hours, but SFA offered a lung-sparing alternative with similar cumulative opioid requirements and patient satisfaction, fewer clinically apparent block-related complications, and a shorter hospital stay. These findings support a risk-benefit framework to guide individualized analgesic selection. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level I. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT from JBJS comparing SFA vs interscalene block for arthroscopic shoulder surgery, addressing a highly clinically relevant perioperative question with noninferiority design and meaningful secondary outcomes including complication rates.
bullets: Surgeon-performed shoulder field anesthesia matched interscalene block for total pain control over 48 hours after arthroscopic shoulder surgery, though the interscalene block gave better relief in the first 4 to 8 hours.

The interscalene block group had two cases of Horner syndrome and one respiratory event requiring ICU care, while shoulder field anesthesia produced none of these complications and led to a shorter hospital stay.

For patients with pulmonary risk or when avoiding phrenic nerve block matters, shoulder field anesthesia is a viable surgeon-administered alternative with equivalent opioid use and patient satisfaction.

candidates.title: Myocardial Infarction Within 6 Months before Total Shoulder Arthroplasty is Strongly Associated with Postoperative Complications.
candidates.authors_short: Parmar RP, Sahni VS, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: As total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) is increasing in volume, limited data exist regarding how recent myocardial infarction (MI) influences postoperative outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of MI timing, type, treatment, and anatomical location on rates of postoperative cardiac, medical, and surgical complications following TSA. METHODS: A national insurance database, PearlDiver, was queried to identify patients with a history of MI within two years prior to TSA. These patients were propensity-matched 1:4 to controls without prior MI based on demographics and comorbidities. The MI cohort was stratified by timing (0-6 months, 6-12 months, 12-18 months, 18-24 months), and subgroup analyses were performed by MI type (Type 1 vs. Type 2), ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) vs Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) classification, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), and infarct location. RESULTS: A history of MI within 2 years preceding TSA had a strong association with higher odds of postoperative MI (OR 5.67; 95% CI, 3.86-8.32). The strongest association was observed when MI occurred within 6 months of TSA (OR 9.95; 95% CI, 6.50-15.24). Type 1 MI was strongly associated with postoperative MI, particularly within 6 months (OR 10.86; 95% CI, 6.96-16.95). Type 2 MI within 6 months was strongly associated with postoperative MI (OR 10.69; 95% CI, 2.50-45.63), DVT (OR 9.81; 95% CI, 2.30-41.79), and PJI (OR 5.24; 95% CI, 1.60-17.18). Both STEMI (OR = 6.17) and NSTEMI (OR = 5.77) were strongly associated with postoperative MI. Anterior MI was strongly associated with postoperative MI (OR 7.22; 95% CI, 3.36-15.49), whereas inferior MI was strongly associated with 90-day mortality (OR 6.46; 95% CI, 1.85-22.60). CONCLUSION: MI within 2 years and specifically 6 months of TSA was associated with higher odds of postoperative complications. MI timing, subtype, treatment, and location should be carefully weighed when considering TSA in this high-risk population.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large NSQIP-based retrospective cohort (n=29,382) with derivation and validation, developing a preoperative bedside tool for non-home discharge after TSA that is directly applicable to surgical planning and patient counseling.
bullets: Patients who had a heart attack within 6 months before total shoulder arthroplasty had nearly 10 times the odds of a postoperative heart attack compared to matched controls.
Both STEMI and NSTEMI carried similar elevated risk, and inferior MI was specifically linked to a sixfold increase in 90-day mortality after total shoulder arthroplasty.
Surgeons should carefully weigh MI timing, type, and location before scheduling total shoulder arthroplasty, as risk remains significantly elevated for up to two years after the cardiac event.

candidates.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty Is Associated With Lower 90-Day Inpatient Readmission Than Hemiarthroplasty for Femoral Neck Fracture in Patients Aged 65-75 Years: A Propensity Score-Matched Nationwide Readmissions Database Study.
candidates.authors_short: Maman D, Steinfeld Y, Berkovich Y
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comparative early hospital-based outcomes of hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty (THA) for femoral neck fracture remain uncertain in patients aged 65-75 years. METHODS: Using the 2022 Nationwide Readmissions Database, we identified patients aged 65-75 years admitted with an acute femoral neck fracture who underwent hemiarthroplasty or THA. Patients were matched 1:1 using exact matching on age, Hospital Frailty Risk Score category, and mental-disorder status, plus propensity-score matching with a 0.20-standard-deviation caliper. The primary outcome was all-cause inpatient readmission within 90 days. RESULTS: Among 8,012 eligible admissions, 5,108 patients underwent hemiarthroplasty and 2,904 underwent THA. Matching yielded 2,702 patients per group, with all postmatch absolute standardized mean differences <0.10. THA was associated with a lower observed 90-day inpatient readmission rate than hemiarthroplasty (10.1% vs 15.7%; odds ratio, 0.60; 95% confidence interval, 0.51-0.71; P < .001). Death during the first readmission was also less frequent after THA (0.1% vs 0.7%; P = .002). A narrowly defined inpatient principal-diagnosis dislocation indicator did not differ significantly between groups and should not be interpreted as overall dislocation incidence. Index and total 90-day hospital charges were higher with THA. CONCLUSIONS: In this observational claims-based study, THA was associated with a lower observed 90-day inpatient readmission rate than hemiarthroplasty. Residual selection bias may partly explain this association, and these findings do not establish a causal benefit of THA. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-matched claims database study (n=77,958) in JBJS-American demonstrating dose-independent SSRI association with periprosthetic fracture, infection, dislocation, and revision after THA, with immediate preoperative counseling implications.
bullets: In patients aged 65 to 75 with femoral neck fracture, THA had a 90-day readmission rate of 10.1% compared to 15.7% for hemiarthroplasty.
Death at first readmission was also lower after THA (0.1% vs 0.7%), though THA carried higher index and total 90-day hospital charges.
For active, younger elderly patients being considered for femoral neck fracture fixation, THA may reduce early readmissions, but selection bias limits causal conclusions.

candidates.title: Mechanical Failure and Revision Risk Following Transition from PFNA to TFNA: A Single-Center Cohort Study of 1,970 Patients.
candidates.authors_short: Ben Zoor I, Fogel I, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, and time to failure between two cephalomedullary nail designs following an institutional transition. METHODS: Design: Retrospective consecutive cohort study. SETTING: Single Level I trauma center, Israel. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged >65 years with acute OTA/AO 31A fractures (subtypes 31A1-31A3) treated with a short cephalomedullary nail with helical blade fixation, either the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) or the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA), between January 2018 and May 2025 were included. Implant type was determined solely by an institutional transition from PFNA to TFNA in March 2023 for logistical reasons rather than surgeon preference. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Implant mechanical failure, cut-out rate, time to failure, body mass index (BMI), and Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) were compared between groups. Mortality within the early revision-risk window was compared between groups to exclude survival bias. RESULTS: The PFNA cohort comprised 1,388 patients (mean age 83.1 years, range 65-102; 986 females [71.0%]) and the TFNA cohort 582 patients (mean age 82.9 years, range 65-107; 407 females [69.9%]); baseline demographics were comparable (age, p=0.691; sex, p=0.626). Orthopedic follow-up was 63.9% for the TFNA cohort versus 61.0% for the PFNA cohort (p=0.24), with a shorter maximum observation period for TFNA (TFNA 26 vs. PFNA 88 months).TFNA was associated with a five-fold increase in implant mechanical failure relative to PFNA (TFNA 1.6% vs. PFNA 0.3%; RR=5.36, 95% CI 1.66-17.3; p=0.005), primarily driven by a four-fold increase in cut-outs (1.2% vs. 0.3%; RR=4.18, 95% CI 1.23-14.2; p=0.027). Failures occurred earlier with TFNA (median 80.0 vs. 244.0 days; p=0.027). Among cut-outs, OTA/AO subtype distribution did not differ (31A1: TFNA 57.1% vs. PFNA 50.0%; no 31A3 in either group; p=1.00); TFNA patients had a higher BMI (median 23.9 vs. 20.1 kg/m 2 ; p=0.024), but mean TAD did not differ (TFNA 24.6 vs. PFNA 21.1 mm; p=0.37). Mortality within the revision-risk window did not differ (TFNA 7.2% vs. PFNA 8.8%; p=0.24). CONCLUSIONS: The transition to the Trochanteric Fixation Nail-Advanced (TFNA) was associated with five-fold higher mechanical failure and four-fold higher cut-out rates than the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) with earlier failures suggesting reduced mechanical stability of the TFNA during early fracture healing. Heightened vigilance is warranted when using TFNA, particularly in patients with higher body mass index early postoperatively. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Propensity-matched national database study comparing THA vs hemiarthroplasty for femoral neck fracture in 65-75 year olds showing significantly lower 90-day readmission with THA, directly informing implant selection in a common high-stakes decision.
bullets: In 1,970 patients over 65 with hip fractures, switching from PFNA to TFNA was associated with a five-fold increase in mechanical failure and a four-fold increase in cut-out rates.
Failures occurred much earlier with TFNA (median 80 days vs. 244 days), suggesting the implant provides less stability during the critical early healing window.
Surgeons using TFNA should increase early postoperative surveillance, especially in heavier patients, and consider whether implant selection affects mechanical outcomes at their own institution.

candidates.title: Predictive Modeling of Clinically Apparent Shoulder Periprosthetic Joint Infection (PJI).
candidates.authors_short: Hsu JE, Ricchetti ET, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The first International Consensus Meeting (ICM) definition of shoulder periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) introduced a tiered framework of PJI categories based on weighting of minor criteria for those cases not having major criteria of Definite infection. The selection of minor criteria and weightings was based on expert opinion and limited available evidence. The purpose of this study was to use prospective, multicenter data to develop a predictive model for clinically apparent shoulder PJI to inform a more evidence-based understanding of minor criteria and PJI categories. METHODS: Prospective data were collected on 861 consecutive revision shoulder arthroplasty cases within the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) Revision Shoulder Arthroplasty and PJI Multicenter Research Group. Presence of a sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis and intra-articular purulence were identified as pathognomonic indicators of infection (major criteria) and used as the primary outcome for multivariable analysis. Logistic regression modeling was performed, with model specification guided by information criteria. Variable selection emphasized optimal model fit while balancing complexity, focusing on: (1) markers of host inflammatory response, (2) universally available and commonly utilized diagnostic tests, (3) minimizing the total number of variables, and (4) preserving model usability despite missing data. RESULTS: Among 861 cases, 97 shoulders (11%) met the outcome of interest (sinus tract or intra-articular purulence). The final model incorporated seven variables spanning clinical findings, laboratory values, imaging, intraoperative assessment, and microbiology. These variables were erythema, unexpected wound drainage, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP), radiographic humeral osteolysis, synovial neutrophils ≥70% or positive frozen section (≥5 polymorphonuclear cells in ≥5 high-powered fields), intraoperative humeral loosening, and ≥2 positive cultures with the same organism. The apparent concordance statistic in the development cohort was 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.94). A nomogram was subsequently developed to estimate the probability of PJI, defined by the presence of a sinus tract or intra-articular purulence. CONCLUSION: Using prospective, multicenter data, this study proposes a seven-factor nomogram to estimate the probability of clinically apparent shoulder PJI. The model showed strong apparent discrimination for clinically apparent infection in the development cohort. External validation will be necessary to confirm performance, and consensus will be required to establish weighting and diagnostic thresholds for tiers of non-definite shoulder PJI.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective multicenter cohort study from PLUTO group evaluating alignment changes after transphyseal ACLR in near-skeletally-mature patients, providing level 2 evidence on iatrogenic growth disturbance risk relevant to pediatric sports practice.
bullets: A seven-factor model using erythema, wound drainage, elevated ESR or CRP, humeral osteolysis on imaging, synovial neutrophils, intraoperative humeral loosening, and two or more positive cultures accurately identified clinically apparent shoulder periprosthetic joint infection in 11% of 861 revision cases.
This tool applies to surgeons evaluating revision shoulder arthroplasty patients who do not clearly meet major infection criteria such as sinus tract or frank purulence.

A nomogram built from these seven variables can guide pre- and intraoperative decision-making for shoulder periprosthetic joint infection, though external validation is still needed before routine clinical adoption.

candidates.title: Defining Long-Term Success After Anatomic Total Shoulder Arthroplasty: Survivorship and Clinically Important Outcomes.
candidates.authors_short: Kucharik MP, Hung V, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Long-term success after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA) is frequently defined by implant survivorship, but revision-free survival may not reflect durable clinical benefit. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of 791 consecutive aTSAs performed between 2003 and 2015 was conducted. Implant survivorship was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Clinical outcomes were evaluated at a 10-year landmark, and clinically important thresholds for the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score were derived using patient satisfaction as the anchor. Multivariable regression identified predictors of revision and substantial clinical benefit (SCB). RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier survivorship was 96.1% at 10 years and 93.7% at 15 years. Walch B glenoid morphology and younger age were independently associated with revision. Clinical outcomes remained improved at long-term follow-up despite gradual attenuation over time. At 10 years, the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) threshold for the ASES score was 68.1, and 69.5% of shoulders achieved it. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and SCB thresholds for the change in ASES score were 14.0 and 39.2, achieved by 79.9% and 55.8% of shoulders, respectively. Younger age, primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, and lower preoperative ASES score were independently associated with achievement of SCB. CONCLUSIONS: aTSA demonstrated excellent long-term implant survivorship and modest patient-reported outcomes, although shoulder function gradually attenuated over extended follow-up. Despite the gradual functional decline, most patients maintained clinically meaningful benefit at 10 years. Younger age and Walch B morphology increased revision risk. Long-term clinically important thresholds provide patient-centered benchmarks for defining durable success. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: Retrospective cohort study with large sample (n=1,970) comparing PFNA vs TFNA cephalomedullary nails for geriatric hip fractures, addressing a clinically significant mechanical failure question during an institutional implant transition.
bullets: Anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty showed 96% implant survival at 10 years and 94% at 15 years, but only 56% of patients achieved substantial clinical benefit by the 10-year mark.
Younger patients and those with Walch B glenoid morphology face higher revision risk after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty.
Functional gains after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty gradually decline over time, so long-term patient counseling should set realistic expectations about durability of improvement.

candidates.title: Gout May Mimic Infection, Even Years After Achilles Tendon Repair.
candidates.authors_short: DeSena TD, Fine-Lease PH, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gout can affect tendons in addition to joints and may clinically resemble infection. The resulting diagnostic uncertainty may lead to surgical intervention or antibiotic treatment, even in patients whose symptoms might be managed medically if gout is recognized earlier. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does late-onset gouty Achilles tendinopathy after prior Achilles tendon repair clinically resemble infection? (2) What diagnostic findings, including crystal analysis of aspirate or surgically obtained material when available, helped establish or support gout rather than infection? (3) What were the outcomes after gout was confirmed or suspected? METHODS: This is a report of 4 patients with a similar presentation. Between April 2021 and June 2024, three surgeons at three academic medical centers identified 4 adult males, aged 42 to 55 years, who developed acute atraumatic Achilles-region pain, swelling, erythema, drainage, fluctuance, or induration 2 to 18 years after open Achilles tendon repair. These presentations raised concern that gout at or near a prior Achilles tendon repair site may mimic infection and lead to unnecessary interventions when gout is not considered early. We do not have an underlying denominator of patients treated for Achilles tendon repair by these surgeons during this period, but we speculate that it is on the order of several hundred. Minimum follow-up was 6 months after the treatment selected for the index Achilles inflammatory presentation. No patients who met these criteria were excluded, and no patients were lost to follow-up before the minimum follow-up interval. To determine whether this presentation clinically resembled infection, we reviewed presenting symptoms and physical examination findings, including pain, swelling, erythema, drainage, fluctuance, induration, fever, constitutional symptoms, and the treating surgeon's initial diagnostic concern. To answer our second question regarding diagnostic findings that established or supported gout rather than infection, we reviewed laboratory studies, imaging, aspiration findings, Gram stain, bacterial cultures, surgical findings, and pathologic evaluation for monosodium urate crystals. To answer our third question regarding outcomes, we reviewed whether patients underwent aspiration, surgical irrigation and debridement, antibiotics, immobilization, antiinflammatory or urate-lowering therapy, rheumatology or infectious disease referral, symptom resolution, recurrence, and complications. Three patients underwent aspiration and/or surgical irrigation and debridement for presumed infection. One patient was treated nonsurgically for suspected gout. RESULTS: In 3 of 4 patients, late-onset gouty Achilles tendinopathy after prior Achilles tendon repair clinically resembled infection; it raised concern for an acute inflammatory or infectious process in all 4 patients. Among the 3 patients treated surgically, chalky tophaceous material was identified adjacent to the Achilles tendon, bacterial cultures were negative, and histological analysis confirmed monosodium urate crystals. The fourth patient had suspected gout based on hyperuricemia, Achilles-region symptoms, and improvement with nonsurgical treatment, although gout was not pathologically confirmed. All patients reported symptom resolution by latest follow-up (6 to 16 months). CONCLUSION: Acute gouty tendinopathy can present years after Achilles tendon repair and can closely mimic postoperative infection, even when serum uric acid is normal. In patients without systemic signs of sepsis, earlier consideration of gout and routine crystal analysis when aspirate or surgically obtained material is available may help avoid unnecessary surgical debridement or prolonged empiric antibiotics when infection is not otherwise supported. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Retrospective cohort study examining radial head arthroplasty vs ORIF in a large Ontario population (n=3,159) with long follow-up showing lower reoperation rates with RHA, highly relevant to elbow trauma surgical decision-making.
bullets: Gout at a prior Achilles repair site can present years later with pain, swelling, erythema, and drainage that looks identical to infection, even with a normal serum uric acid.
In patients without systemic sepsis signs, sending any aspirated or surgical material for crystal analysis can confirm gout and avoid unnecessary debridement or prolonged antibiotics.

All four patients in this series resolved with appropriate treatment once gout was identified, supporting early consideration of gout in any post-repair Achilles flare without a clear infectious source.

candidates.title: The use of patellar tendon autograft and lateral meniscus repair are associated with loss of motion of the knee among female patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
candidates.authors_short: Dadoo S, Nash AE, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To conduct a sex-stratified analysis of factors associated with subsequent surgery for loss of motion after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), including meniscus repair and graft type. METHODS: All individuals age ≥14 years who underwent primary ACLR between 2014 and 2021 were reviewed. Exclusion criteria included <6 months follow-up and concomitant meniscal root, multiligament, osteochondral or osteotomy procedures. The primary outcome was subsequent surgery for loss of motion. Demographic and surgical variables were compared between individuals who underwent subsequent surgery for loss of motion versus not, for the full cohort and among females and males separately. Significance was set to p < 0.050. RESULTS: A total of 1226 individuals (age: 25 ± 10 years; 49% female) were included at a mean follow-up of 2.3 years. The rate of subsequent surgery for loss of motion was 9.0% for the full cohort, 12.3% for females and 5.9% for males. Among the full cohort, female sex (OR: 2.31; p < 0.001) and lateral meniscus (LM) repair (OR: 1.62; p = 0.048) were predictors of subsequent surgery for loss of motion. Among females, bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft use (OR: 1.91; p = 0.034) and LM repair (OR: 1.72; p = 0.046) were predictors of subsequent surgery for loss of motion, with combined BPTB autograft use and LM repair resulting in a significantly higher rate of subsequent surgery for loss of motion (32% vs. 12%; p = 0.004). Among males, graft type and meniscus repair were not associated with subsequent surgery for loss of motion (both p > 0.050). CONCLUSION: In this sex-stratified analysis, BPTB autograft use and LM repair were identified as factors predictive of subsequent surgery for loss of motion after primary ACLR when analysing females independently, while no predictive factors were identified when analysing males independently. Understanding factors associated with loss of motion after primary ACLR among males and females separately may guide individualised surgical decision-making and patient counselling. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large retrospective cohort (n=3,383 TKAs) examining patellar resurfacing vs non-resurfacing and peripatellar injury rates, directly addressing a common intraoperative decision with meaningful complication implications.
bullets: Female patients undergoing ACL reconstruction have twice the rate of subsequent surgery for stiffness compared to males (12% vs 6%).
In female patients, patellar tendon autograft combined with lateral meniscus repair raises the stiffness reoperation rate to 32%, versus 12% with neither factor.
Graft type and meniscus repair do not predict stiffness reoperation in male patients, so this risk-stratification applies to female patients only.
